Body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs) including skin picking affect an estimated 1–5% of the general population — and significantly higher rates among children with autism spectrum disorder, anxiety disorders, and ADHD. In India alone, with 18 million children on the autism spectrum, BFRB-related challenges affect tens of millions of families. The shame families carry is not matched by the prevalence of the experience.

This Is a Wiring Difference. Not a Behavior Choice.
The Brain Regions Involved
Somatosensory Cortex
Processes tactile input; in some children, under-amplifies routine touch, creating a constant search for richer sensory input
Basal Ganglia
Governs habitual, automatic behaviors; skin picking becomes embedded here as a regulatory loop
Prefrontal Cortex
Responsible for impulse control and awareness; in children with ADHD and autism, this system matures later — meaning picking often happens before conscious awareness registers
Limbic System (Amygdala)
When anxiety activates the amygdala, the basal ganglia's habitual picking response fires as a tension-relief mechanism
Plain English for Parents
Your child's brain has found a shortcut. When the nervous system needs regulation — more sensory input, less anxiety, a moment of focused calm — the fingers know exactly where to go. This pathway has been used thousands of times. It works. That's why "just stop" never works: you're asking the brain to abandon a solution that reliably delivers relief.
What we need is not elimination — it's replacement. Give the fingers a new solution that meets the same need. Over time, the new pathway becomes the default.
"The picking isn't the problem. The picking is the nervous system's answer to a problem we haven't solved yet."
Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020): Comprehensive neurological framework for sensory processing treatment in ASD. DOI: 10.3389/fnint.2020.556660 | Habit reversal therapy evidence: PMC4865185

Sensory Redirection for Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors (BFRB)
Give the Fingers Somewhere Else to Go
Skin picking (excoriation disorder / dermatillomania) is a Body-Focused Repetitive Behavior (BFRB) in which the child repeatedly picks at their own skin — often at scabs, bumps, blemishes, or imperfections — resulting in wounds that don't heal, scarring, and significant emotional distress. The behavior typically occurs outside conscious awareness and serves a regulatory function: it provides sensory input, reduces anxiety, induces a focused state, or manages emotional overwhelm. It is not a choice, not attention-seeking, and not a discipline problem.
Sensory Redirection is the evidence-based approach of replacing the picking behavior with materials that meet the same underlying need — giving the nervous system what it's searching for, through a safe and constructive channel. The 9 materials on this page represent the full spectrum of BFRB functions: tactile seeking, peeling, tension discharge, barriers, anxiety relief, awareness, skin healing, hand occupation, and competing responses.

This Technique Crosses Every Therapy Boundary
Occupational Therapy (OT) — Primary Lead
Conducts sensory processing evaluation to identify the specific function of picking. Selects and prescribes materials matched to the child's sensory profile. Teaches proper implementation and builds home toolkit.
ABA / BCBA — Behavioral Architecture
Conducts functional behavior assessment (FBA) to identify antecedents, functions, and consequences. Designs competing response protocols, reinforcement schedules, and data collection systems. Integrates with ComB framework.
NeuroDevelopmental Pediatrics — Medical Oversight
Rules out dermatological causes, assesses for co-occurring anxiety/OCD requiring medication, monitors wound infections, and coordinates multi-disciplinary approach. Provides diagnosis of excoriation disorder when warranted.
Special Education (SpEd) — School Integration
Ensures picking management strategies transfer to school settings. Provides classroom fidget access, communicates with teachers, and builds IEP accommodations. Eliminates shame-based school responses.
"The brain doesn't organize itself by therapy type. Skin picking sits at the intersection of sensory processing (OT), behavioral function (ABA), developmental neurology (NeuroDev), and educational adjustment (SpEd). Our FusionModule™ coordinates all four simultaneously." — Pinnacle Blooms Consortium Clinical Team

Read This Before Using Any Material.
🟢 GREEN — Safe to Proceed
  • Child is in a calm, regulated baseline state
  • No active skin infections on picking sites
  • Material has been checked for allergy (putty, adhesives, latex)
  • Child is willing (not forced) to engage
  • Parent/caregiver is calm, non-judgmental, curious
  • Materials are appropriate for child's age and developmental level
🟡 AMBER — Modify Before Proceeding
  • Mild skin irritation → use barrier and skin care first
  • Child refuses specific materials → try alternatives from the 9
  • Picking has increased recently → identify stressor first
  • Child is dysregulated → use calming strategy first, then materials
🔴 RED — Stop and Seek Professional Guidance
  • Wounds become infected (spreading redness, warmth, pus, fever) → Medical attention immediately
  • Picking involves intent to cause pain or self-harm → Immediate psychology consult
  • Picking has suddenly intensified significantly without clear trigger → Professional assessment
  • Child is severely distressed and daily life significantly impacted → BFRB specialist referral
  • Multiple BFRB behaviors emerging simultaneously → Comprehensive assessment warranted
Material Safety Specifics
  • Putty/dough: Non-toxic only; check for wheat allergy (flour-based DIY)
  • Adhesive barriers: Hypoallergenic for sensitive skin; never apply tightly
  • Textured stones: No sharp edges; no small detachable parts for ages under 4
  • Aromatherapy: Diluted only, never undiluted essential oils on skin

The Right Environment Makes This 3× More Effective.
Setup Checklist
  • Identify the 3 highest-risk locations where picking most often occurs (TV couch, homework desk, bed)
  • Place alternative materials at each location before picking typically occurs — not after
  • Small mirror placed where picking happens most
  • Awareness bracelet on wrist before entering high-risk activities
  • Remove or cover loose skin at pick sites with barrier if appropriate
  • Skin care station at bathroom mirror — moisturizer visible and accessible
  • Distractions reduced during initial material introduction sessions
  • Caregiver agreement on gentle signal word (not "stop picking!")

Alternatives Closer Than Skin

No Shame, No Surveillance

ACT III: THE EXECUTION
Check every item before beginning. Your child's readiness — and yours — directly determines whether this session becomes a positive experience or a missed opportunity.
Child has eaten in the last 2 hours
Child is not showing signs of illness (fever, fatigue, pain)
No major meltdown or escalation in the past 30 minutes
Child is alert and not half-asleep
Active wounds are not infected
Caregiver is calm (not frustrated about picking today)
Alternative materials are in place and accessible
🟢 All Checked — GO
Proceed to Step 1: The Invitation
🟡 1–2 Unchecked — MODIFY
Skip formal session. Place one material (picking stone or putty) near the child without instruction. No pressure. Presence = success today.
🔴 3+ Unchecked — POSTPONE
Run the cool-down activity first. Offer a drink and a snack. Come back to materials in 20 minutes. If the day is too difficult — postpone and record why. The data matters.
"The best session is the one that starts when both the child and caregiver are ready. A 5-minute successful session is infinitely more valuable than a 20-minute forced one."
ABA Antecedent Manipulation: Setting event management directly determines intervention effectiveness. Core component of behavioral session protocols.
STEP 1 OF 6
Begin With an Invitation, Not a Command.
Timing: 30–60 seconds | What You're Doing: Introducing the alternative material through play and curiosity — not instructions. The child should feel the material has appeared for them to explore, not been assigned as a task.
Exact Words to Use
"Hey, I found something interesting. Want to see?"
[Place the material in front of the child — don't hand it]
"It's got a really interesting texture. I keep wanting to touch it."
[Touch it yourself, demonstrating interest]
Body Language
  • Sit beside the child, not in front (less confrontational)
  • Relaxed posture — don't lean in
  • Let your hands explore the material casually
  • Smile genuinely — this is curiosity, not therapy
What Acceptance Looks Like
  • Child glances at the material
  • Child reaches out to touch it without prompting
  • Child picks it up
  • Child continues what they were doing while holding it
What Resistance Looks Like
  • Child ignores it → Wait 2 minutes, try a different material
  • Child pushes it away → Retrieve it calmly; try again tomorrow
  • Child says "no" → Honor that; try during a different activity tomorrow

Never force. An alternative that's been forced will be rejected. The goal is that the child chooses it because it satisfies them — not because they've been told to use it.
STEP 2 OF 6
The Material Meets the Need.
Timing: 1–3 minutes | What You're Doing: Once the child has touched or picked up the material, deepen engagement by naming what you notice — without directing. Guide through observation, not instruction.
Script
"That bumpy part feels really different, doesn't it." [statement, not question]
"I wonder what the other side feels like."
"Can you make it go flat? I bet your fingers are strong enough." [if child is using putty]
Reinforcement Timing
  • When to praise: When child interacts with material for any duration (even 5 seconds)
  • What to say: "You're using that so well." or simply "Yeah." with a warm nod
  • What NOT to say: Don't reference picking. Just reinforce the present engagement.
Child Response Spectrum
Ideal
Sustained focused engagement with the material, picking forgotten
Acceptable
Brief exploration, material discarded — hands occupied for even 30 seconds before drifting to skin. Record as partial success.
Concerning
Child becomes agitated or distressed by the material → Remove immediately, note texture/resistance level, try softer alternative
PMC11506176: Structured material introduction with reinforcement meets evidence-based practice criteria for ASD (PRISMA systematic review, 2024)
STEP 3 OF 6
This Is the Active Ingredient.
Timing: 3–10 minutes (or as long as naturally sustained) | The child uses the alternative material in the specific way that matches their picking function.
Tactile-Seeking Function
Child scans, explores, and maps the texture of the picking stone — fingers moving the way they move on skin, satisfying the same tactile search. No instruction needed. The material does the work.
Peeling Function
Child peels dried glue from palm, removes stickers one by one. The satisfaction of lifting, removing, and peeling — exactly as experienced with skin.
Anxiety-Discharge Function
Child squeezes stress tool, uses weighted lap pad, or practices breathing with the Hoberman sphere. Tension releases through a tool, not skin.
Understimulation Function
Child engages with fine motor kit or putty during TV/homework — hands occupied, sensory pathway fed, picking opportunity eliminated.
Automatic/Habitual Function
Competing response tools: child practices clenching fists or gripping stress ball for 90 seconds when the awareness bracelet signals an urge.
Common Execution Errors
  • ❌ Redirecting the child every time they move toward skin → Instead: offer the material; don't police
  • ❌ Stopping the session when the child picks despite having the material → Instead: note it as data and continue
  • ❌ Introducing multiple materials at once → Instead: one material per session until pattern emerges
PMC10955541: 40-minute therapy sessions maximally effective. Home sessions 10–20 minutes; therapeutic action occupies 40–60% of session time.
STEP 4 OF 6
3 Good Reps > 10 Forced Ones.
Timing: Additional 2–5 minutes | Repetition Target: Child uses the material 3–5 times across the session. Material accessible during all high-risk periods — not just formal "sessions."
Week 1–2
Single material passively available. No instruction, just presence. Note which materials child engages with.
Week 3–4
Multiple materials accessible; child chooses. Gentle naming: "Your picking stone is here." Increase variety within successful category.
Week 5–8
Child selects and reaches independently. Competing response practiced deliberately. Introduce new category (e.g., add peeling to texture).
Satiation Indicators (child has had enough for now)
  • Child puts the material down and doesn't return to it
  • Child becomes restless or distracted
  • Child moves on to another activity

These are normal. End the material exposure naturally — never force continuation.
Sensory integration therapy dosage: 2–3 sessions/week for 8–12 weeks as typical protocol. Session-level repetition from clinical consensus and Pinnacle protocols.
STEP 5 OF 6
Celebrate the Attempt. Not Just the Success.
Timing: Within 3 seconds of alternative material use

Natural Consequence
The skin heals. The scars fade. The arms show again.

What NOT to Do

STEP 6 OF 6
No Session Ends Abruptly.
Timing: 1–2 minutes | Every session closes with a gentle, predictable ritual that signals completion without abrupt withdrawal.
Transition Warning (2 minutes before ending)

"Two more minutes with your putty, then we're putting it away until tomorrow." Visual Timer — Pinnacle Transition Object: ₹425 on Amazon.in →
Cool-Down Activity (choose one)
  • Slow, deep hand massage with moisturizer (skin care + sensory + cool-down combined)
  • Three deep breaths together (count to 4 in, 4 out)
  • Putting materials away together — a ritual of closure
  • Transition to preferred quiet activity
Material Put-Away Ritual
Child places the material in "its spot" — this creates ownership and anticipation of using it again.
"The picking stone lives here. You can get it whenever you need it."
If Child Resists Ending
  • Don't force material removal if child is calm and engaged — extension is fine
  • Use visual countdown: "3... 2... 1... all done for now"
  • Transition object in hand if needed

Session Abandonment Is Not Failure. It's Data.
❓ "My child ignores every material I introduce."
The function hasn't been matched yet. Observe picking closely for 3 days: is it texture-seeking, peeling, or anxiety? Mismatch = rejection. The right material creates immediate interest.
❓ "My child picks while holding the alternative material."
This is progress, not failure. The material is building a new pathway. Over 2–3 weeks, picking while holding reduces as the material becomes preferred. Don't remove the material — increase its quality.
❓ "My child removes every barrier I put on."
The barrier is the wrong type, wrong placement, or wasn't the child's choice. Involve the child in choosing the barrier style. Try a softer option. Never use barriers punitively.
❓ "My child gets more agitated when I try to redirect."
Redirection feels like interruption. Stop redirecting verbally. Simply place materials within reach without comment. Let the child discover them without associating them with "instead of picking."
❓ "There's no change after 3 weeks."
3 weeks is early. Check: (a) Are materials within immediate reach? (b) Is the correct function targeted? (c) Are you tracking? Seek OT consultation to identify the specific sensory function.
❓ "The picking is worse since we started."
Increased picking during the first 1–2 weeks can reflect an extinction burst — the old behavior intensifying briefly as the new pathway forms. Hold steady. Seek OT guidance if persisting beyond 3 weeks.

  • No cognitive strategies needed
  • Parent-managed materials placement
  • Minimum pressure, maximum access
Ages 7–10

Profile-Based Variations
Sensory Seeker Profile
Child picks for texture/tactile input → Prioritize: Picking stones + Peeling alternatives + Putty. Target sensory richness. The more varied the textures, the better.
Anxiety Profile
Child picks when stressed/overwhelmed → Prioritize: Weighted tools + Breathing + Stress balls. Target the anxiety first. BFRB reduces as anxiety decreases.
Understimulation Profile
Child picks during passive activities → Prioritize: Fine motor kits + Putty for TV time. Target hand occupation proactively.
Automatic/Habitual Profile
Child picks without awareness → Prioritize: Awareness tools + Competing responses. Target awareness as Step 1 of everything else.
ACT IV: THE PROGRESS ARC
Phase: Introduction
Patience Is a Therapeutic Tool.
15%
Week 1–2 Progress
Introduction phase — neural pathways just beginning to form
In Weeks 1–2, Look For:
Child tolerates alternative material in their environment (even if not using it)
Child touches or explores at least one material independently (even briefly)
Picking may continue at same frequency — this is expected and not failure
Child does NOT resist caregiver placing materials nearby
One or two moments of spontaneous alternative use — celebrate these disproportionately

Parent Emotional Preparation: Weeks 1–2 are the hardest. The old behavior continues. The new pathway has barely begun. This is not evidence that the approach doesn't work — it's evidence that neural pathways take time to establish. The behavior that took years to build will not change in 14 days.
"If my child holds a picking stone for 10 seconds longer today than yesterday — that is real, measurable neural progress."
PMC11506176: Sensory integration intervention outcomes emerge across 8–12 week timelines. Early-phase indicators focus on tolerance and participation.
Phase: Consolidation
Neural Pathways Are Forming. Here's What That Looks Like.
40%

Consolidation phase — first spontaneous moments of alternative use appearing
In Weeks 3–4, Look For:

Awareness bracelet starts functioning — child occasionally touches it before picking

ACT V: COMMUNITY & ECOSYSTEM
From the Therapist's Notes.
Priya, Hyderabad | Son, Age 8, ASD + ADHD
Before: Arms covered in scabs from constant picking during TV time. Father would raise his voice; son would cry; picking would intensify. OT assessment revealed: understimulation function — hands were idle and seeking input.
Intervention: Sensory putty with embedded beads placed on the couch arm. No instruction. Just there.
Week 3: Son was seen extracting beads from putty during a cartoon — completely absorbed. Zero picking during that 45-minute session.
Outcome (8 weeks): Picking episodes reduced by approximately 70% during screen time. Existing wounds healed. Father stopped raising his voice because the confrontation trigger was removed.
Sunita, Bengaluru | Daughter, Age 11, Anxiety + Sensory Differences
Before: Daughter picking at her scalp and arms during homework. Shame was profound — she wore full sleeves in 40°C heat.
Intervention: Awareness bracelet (beaded) + peeling alternatives (school glue on palm for after-school homework time). Competing response taught by BCBA.
Week 6: Daughter reported: "When I feel like picking, I peel the glue first. Usually the urge goes away."
Outcome (12 weeks): Scalp healed. Arms visible. School performance improved as anxiety-picking cycle was interrupted. Daughter developed vocabulary for her sensory needs.

1. BFRB Evidence Base (PMC4865185)
BFRBs confirmed as regulatory behaviors serving sensory, emotional, and anxiety functions. Habit Reversal Therapy and ComB treatment show 40–70% reduction in BFRB frequency in RCTs. → Read on PubMed: PMC4865185

16 studies (2013–2023) confirm sensory integration intervention meets criteria as evidence-based practice for ASD. Directly supports sensory alternative approach for BFRB. → Read on PubMed: PMC11506176

Every Question. Answered.
ACT VI: THE CLOSE & LOOP
❓ How long before I see a reduction in picking?
Most families see meaningful reduction between weeks 4 and 8 when the correct functional match is made. If you haven't seen any change by week 6, the function hasn't been correctly identified — seek OT consultation for a sensory profile assessment.
❓ Is skin picking a sign of autism?
Skin picking (BFRB) is significantly more prevalent in children with autism, ADHD, and anxiety disorders, but also occurs in neurotypical children. The presence of skin picking warrants a developmental assessment to identify any underlying conditions. Call 9100 181 181 for a free consultation.
❓ My child picks in their sleep. Can these materials help?
Nocturnal picking reflects extremely automatic behavior. Barrier methods (soft finger covers or arm sleeves worn to sleep) are most effective for sleep-time picking, combined with moisturizer application as part of the bedtime routine. Awareness tools are less effective during sleep.
❓ Should I show my child this page?
For children ages 10 and above, yes — with your guidance. Self-understanding reduces shame dramatically. Children who understand "my brain is searching for regulation" stop feeling broken. Reading Cards 03 and 06 together can be transformative.
❓ Is it normal for picking to get worse before it gets better?
Yes. An extinction burst — brief intensification of the old behavior as the new pathway forms — is documented in BFRB literature. It typically lasts 1–2 weeks. Hold steady. If it persists beyond 3 weeks without signs of the new pathway forming, seek guidance.
❓ My child picks at multiple sites. Do I need different materials for each?
No. The function is usually consistent across picking sites. One well-matched material — used wherever picking occurs — addresses the function regardless of where it manifests on the body.
❓ Can adults use these materials too?
Absolutely. While this page is designed for children (ages 4–14), all 9 materials apply equally to adolescents and adults with skin picking. The protocol adaptations for ages 11–14 extend naturally to adult use.
